utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no preliminaries, we will move into closed session. But first, Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We now turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. We take a break, and we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00. Mr. Groome, is the next witness ready by then?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, we start now again, so no further talking. Yes. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. The Prosecution had requested leave to reply to the Defence response to the 92 ter motion. Leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps while we wait for the witness we can address one preliminary issue we had with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I was saying while we wit for the witness there was one preliminary matter we wanted to bring to the attention of the Court and to ask for additional guidance. The Prosecution modified the 65 ter summary for the present witness, and we believe not entirely in compliance with the Chamber's guidance of 24 August 2012, where it was clearly stated that for the purpose of amending 65 ter witness summaries, it is sufficient for the party to provide the opposing party and the Chamber with adequate notice of such amendments as soon as possible and in any event sufficiently in advance of the witness's testimony. Defence notes that it received an e-mail on Sunday, December the 2nd, 2012, at 6.35 p.m. for this witness with three new topics for the 65 ter summary and two new 65 ter documents of exhibits. This is more -- not more than a couple days before the testimony of the witness, and this testimony has been scheduled for at least two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'd rather first welcome the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest, and Mr. Fraser, I'm sorry, but a procedural issue was raised immediately before you entered the court. That's the reason why we do not start yet. I suggest to the parties that the new areas are not covered within the first session. Is that a possibility? I have not looked at it, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I would rather address the Court on the issue now, Your Honours. These are areas that would be addressed in the first session, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's do the following. Mr. Fraser, if you wouldn't mind, we first resolve the matter which may affect the examination-in-chief. And if you would have patience with us, I'll ask you after we heard the parties, the parties' submissions, we'll ask you to make a solemn declaration and then we'll start with your testimony. Apologies for this course of proceeding. Mr. Ivetic, please complete your submission which I interrupted a minute ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We believe that although with this witness it should not make a difference with the new topics, we're prepared for them, but the guidance thus far that has been in place has been to sufficiently in advance of the witness's testimony give notice of any amendments to the 65 ter summary, and we believe in this case where the amendments come from a statement that was the result of discussions in July of 2012 and a statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you. I heard you say we believe that although with this witness it should not make a difference with the new topics because you're prepared for them. Does that mean that you want to put the Prosecution on notice that next time you might object? Let's not let -- let's not have this witness to wait for what we'll do in the future because I do understand that for this occasion you do not object, and we'd like to hear from you for future occasions immediately after we've heard the evidence of the witness if that's okay with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Ms. Bolton, you will hear later from Mr. Ivetic why you shouldn't do again what you have done now, but let's first focus on the evidence of this witness. Mr. Fraser, could I invite you to make the solemn declaration of which the text is now handed out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated. Mr. Fraser, you'll first be examined by Ms. Bolton. Ms. Bolton is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm just going to start by reminding you that there are translators at work in the courtroom, and it's important, therefore, that you and I try not to speak too quickly, and if we can in particular try to pause between my questions and your answers that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 82590 [sic], please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, you should see before you a document titled "Witness Statement." Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And scrolling down on the English version of this document, do you recognise the signature that appears on page 1 of the English version?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That would be mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could I ask that we turn to page 39 in the English version only.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again we see a signature on this statement. Do you recognise that signature?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Whose is it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That would be mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The -- is this a copy, sir, of the statement that you provided to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And for the record, the date on this statement, it was signed on the 3rd of December, 2012. However, I'm going to suggest that the statement of 3rd December 2012 was identical in content to a statement you had previously signed on the 2nd of October, 2012, with the exception that the diacritics in the earlier statement appeared as brackets and punctuation marks.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you've had an opportunity, sir, to review this statement during meetings with the Prosecution leading up to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter 28601.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take the opportunity, Ms. Bolton, to put on the record that we looked until now at 289 -- 590, whereas in page 32, line 23, it appears under a different number, and whether you misspoke or whether it's a transcription mistake, I do not know, but it should be 28590. And we now move to 28601.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, you should see before you a one-page document, and if we could scroll to the bottom of this document. There is a signature and date. Whose signature appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is this a document setting out clarifications and corrections to the statement we were just looking at, being 65 ter 28590?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And taking into account those corrections and clarifications, does the statement you've provided to the Office of the Prosecution accurately reflect the information you've provided to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked similar questions today to those posed at the time of your giving your original statement, would your answers be substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And having now taken the solemn affirmation in this court, do you solemnly affirm the truthfulness of your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that both exhibit 28590 and the corrections, 65 ter 28601, be introduced as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 28590 will be Exhibit P576, and 65 ter 28601 will be Exhibit P577.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P576 and P577 are admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I would also ask at this time, Your Honour, there were with respect to the response filed by the Defence with respect to the admission of the associated exhibits only three exhibits that were objected to in substance, although they did object to the total number being 21, and I would ask the admission of all the exhibits, associated exhibits, except for the three objected to which I would propose to deal with at the end of my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be fine, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll invite Madam Registrar to prepare a list and provisionally assign numbers so they are reserved, and meanwhile, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. If I may assist Madam Registrar by indicating the 65 ter numbers of the three exhibits I understood the Defence to be objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please name them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Those are 65 ter 11189, 09741, and 08735.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have all the other numbers, Madam Registrar, of associated exhibits?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I do, including the three that are objected to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With the Court's permission may I read a summary of the witness's evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may so, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Major-General David Fraser served with the Canadian Armed Forces for 37 years, achieving the third highest rank available in the Canadian military. From the 17th of April, 1995, until the 26th of May, 1995, General Fraser served as military assistant to the commander for UNPROFOR forces in Sector Sarajevo, serving first under General Soubirou then under General Gobillard. Sorry, his dates of service were from April 1994 till May 1995. At that time, there were approximately 4.000 UN soldiers serving in Sector Sarajevo. Their duties included ensuring freedom of movement for humanitarian aid, monitoring adherence with the February 1994 cease-fire agreement, monitoring of the weapons collection points established pursuant to that agreement, performing anti-sniping duties, conducting investigations into civilian casualties and deaths from shelling and sniping and protesting those incidents. While serving in Sarajevo, General Fraser met with high-ranking members of both warring factions including both military -- members of the military and politicians. He met General Mladic in person on a few occasions and in addition, he was regularly present during teleconference calls in which General Mladic was a participant. It was clear from General Fraser's dealings with General Mladic's subordinates including both Generals Mladic and Milosevic that there was an effective command and control structure in place and that General Mladic was at the top of the command chain. General Fraser made observations during his time in Sarajevo about artillery fire and sniping fire. He reached the conclusion in terms of sniping that the VRS was intentionally targeting civilians. In terms of shelling, he observed that some of the shelling by the VRS was in response to provocations from the ABiH. Generally speaking, however, that response was disproportionate and random, and for every outgoing ABiH shell the BSA would generally launch ten shells in response. Finally, during General Fraser's time in Sarajevo, he noticed the BSA began to use modified air bombs. It was his opinion that those weapons lacked any military value. That's the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have any further questions, you may put them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I please have 65 ter 17690, page 1 in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You should see before you, sir, a document. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is dated the 19th of September, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Further down the subject title reads, "Press release, 22nd September 1994." What does that suggest to you about the date of the 19th September 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This is an advisory of a press release that's going to go out on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. And the releasing officer here?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Would be me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could we turn to the second page in both English and B/C/S. Could we focus on the last paragraph in English on this page and you'll need to go to page 3 in the B/C/S version to find that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could just take a moment and read this to yourself, sir. Sir, would you agree with me that this is a document explaining the reasons that some NATO air-strikes were requested and carried out?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who was it that called for those air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The UN called for the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And does the document indicate who specifically within the UN or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I don't see in the document who actually called. It was the UN that requested these calls -- the strikes though.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 17690 will be Exhibit P578.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I ask for Exhibit 65 ter 10737, please. May I ask, Your Honours, if the witness could have a hard copy of his statement to assist him in following along during cross -- during examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Assuming that the Defence has no objection, it may be --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you questions about paragraph 142 of your statement, sir, and I'll read you the portion I'm interested in, but please feel free, if it assists you, to turn to the paragraph as well. At paragraph 142, you indicate, and I'll quote: "On the 23rd September 1994, I was present at a meeting between General Mladic and General Brinkman. General Mladic made it clear during that meeting that he controlled what happened in Sarajevo. General Mladic was insensed over the air-strikes and demanded an apology. When no apology was forthcoming he threatened to stop all convoys from entering Sarajevo. He carried through with this threat and closed all check-points in Bosnian Serb territory for a time." What air-strikes was General Mladic upset about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: He was referring to the air-strikes referenced in the previous document you had me look at.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if I could now ask you to look at the document that's before you on the screen. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What organisation is this document from?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It's from the UN headquarters in Sarajevo that General Rose had commanded, and it's from General Brinkman, his Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that we please focus in on the text on page 1 in the English version under "Message." And in the B/C/S version, I believe you'd scroll down the page. I believe you may have to turn the page. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General Brinkman indicates there: "During a telephone conversation that I had yesterday at 2000 H," I take it, "with the BSA commander General Mladic, he threatened to attack UNPROFOR with the same degree of warning that was given to him by UNPROFOR at 22nd September '94. This attack is to take place if UNPROFOR don't respond to the BSA in a satisfactory manner within 24 hours." And then at paragraph 3 is an indication: "In a letter to BHC HQ last evenly (23rd September) BSA HQ announced that they would not approve any movement on BSA territory or by helicopter and therefore allow the activities of UNPROFOR on its territory until the BSA has been able to assess the situation. This will have a major impact on convoys and liaison into Sarajevo and the enclaves." My questions for you, sir, are: Is this the same or a different meeting as the meeting you were discussing in paragraph 142 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General Brinkman's facsimile suggests that this was a conversation that took place over the telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how is it that if General Brinkman was speaking to General Mladic on the phone that you could hear what both parties were saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Use speaker-phones back then so people could hear and take notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was this the only occasion when you participated in a speaker-telephone conversation in which General Mladic was a participant?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No. There were other ones where I listened in on with General Rose or with my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Any idea how often or how many there might have been.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can't give you a specific number, but it was more than three or four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that this document be introduced as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 10737 will be Exhibit P579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted under that number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to turn to the topic/discussion at paragraphs, sort of, 30 to 38 of your statement which is where you set out some of your general observations of General Mladic's interactions with his subordinates, including General Galic and General Milosevic. You indicate that you made observations of the interactions of General Galic and Mladic at paragraph 33 and that they appeared to work well together. Do you recall when it was you had occasion to see the two men together?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would have been probably at the airport at some of the meetings we had.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What were those meetings about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We would talk about cease-fire violations, ongoing situations, trying to ameliorate the situation around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you have occasion also to see General Mladic directly interact with General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I believe I did. Same thing. It was clear from my observations with both Generals Galic and Milosevic that it was General Mladic -- was the -- the commander. He had effective command and control over them and they responded to his direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is it that you base that -- that on?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: On our conversations and discussions from the sector level with the two generals in question about freedom of movement, sniping incidents, cease-fire violations. At times both those generals would have no latitude and would not be able to respond to our protests because they were indicating that it was from a direction that they had received, and in some cases they had a little bit of flexibility on maybe some sniping. And again we could tell from the dialogue with them that there was a structure above them that was controlling their actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of them -- occasions when they indicated that these were matters outside of their control and that they were being directed from somebody else, did they indicate who was directing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In many cases they would indicate, yes, that the -- their headquarters, and General Mladic was -- you know, they were following the orders given to them by him and his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there ever any occasions during your conversations with either General Galic or General Milosevic when they questioned an order or direction they had received from their headquarters or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Nothing that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Or any occasions when they appeared to be acting contrary to those orders or directions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Nothing that comes to mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You allude to paragraph 34 to a discussion you had with General Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I would ask that perhaps we go into closed session briefly for this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session. Would that do, Ms. Bolton?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Private, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You had indicated, sir, that you had a conversation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to deal with a topic you discuss at paragraphs 126 to 135 of your statement, which is the issue of modified air bombs. Was there ever an occasion during your time in Sarajevo when you had the opportunity to either hear or see a modified air bomb in flight?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I never personally saw or heard one. I only read the reports that came in from the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recall what time period it was when you first started to receive reports about these weapons?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would have been sometime in the spring of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Based on the information that you were receiving, what was the description in terms of the sound that these weapons made?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It -- or it was clearly something you could hear and something that you could see because of just the sheer size of this thing going through the air, and it was something quite different than what we had experienced before, and the explosion -- resulting explosion was significantly louder with more devastating effects on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicate at paragraph 126 of your statement that as far as you were concerned, modified air bombs had no military value. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In the context of Sarajevo being a densely populated city, the use of these systems that first were jerry-rigged had no guidance, they were just kind of pointed and fired. You could not control the point of impact, and quite frankly, firing one of these things into a densely populated city, there is no military purpose for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'd like to have 65 ter 18616, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a document, sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we scroll down in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It purports to have been signed by Colonel Tadija Manojlovic, hear of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we scroll up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's addressed from the colonel of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and it's dated April 26, 1995. I'm going to quote you some portions of the text, the body of the text, and then I'll have some questions for you. It states in the document: "In the morning briefing on the 26th of April, 1995, a decision has been taken to hit the village of Donji Kotorac (tunnel entry)." It goes on to say that: "Firing should have commenced in the early evening hours, and the necessary preparations for the firing operation performed beforehand. "The detailed estimate of all structures in the immediate vicinity of the tunnel entrance has been performed from the observation post on Ilinjaca. The measuring" -- I'm skipping topographic point 655. "The measuring performed with instruments indicated that two UNPROFOR check-points are located, at most, 200 metres away while the UNPROFOR observers are constantly communicating through Donji Kotorac from their observation points. Our forward end is located some 500 metres away from the tunnel entrance and the direction of fire is via Kula restaurant." He then states a little later in the document that: "I gave up as the firing would have endangered our forces and UN forces." And finishes by saying: "The commander will brief you on other matters upon his arrival at the command." Were you acquainted with a tunnel in the location of Donji Kotorac?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And where is that tunnel relative to the Butmir airport?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is just across from the airport. It was on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there in fact UNPROFOR check-points located approximately 200 metres away from the tunnel entrance?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there was. It was just entering right into the airport.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the reference in the document to the fact that UNPROFOR observers are constantly communicating through Donji Kotorac, is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. UN forces would traverse the airport and transit in front of the tunnel entrance going through that side of the -- of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was there, in fact, an SRK forward end or front line located approximately 500 metres from that tunnel entrance?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The statement that "the head of artillery gave up on the firing as it would have endangered our forces and UN forces," what does that tell you about the accuracy of the weapon they were contemplating using?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Well, it is indicative that the head of artillery understood some of the characteristics of the weapon system. He did deliberate planning for a potential use of this weapon system against this target, and at the very least there is -- there is a 500 metre probability of error for the beaten zone of this weapon system. If he was not prepared to fire it because of the danger to his own troops. It was not a very accurate weapon system.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How would that compare with, for example, the beaten zone for a direct fire weapon like a tank.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would be like using an scalpel or a butter knife. A tank would be much, much more accurate that you put it in within probably inches or a foot of your -- where you're aiming and this was clearly, at the very least, 500 metres from where you would aim it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I ask that this be tendered as the next exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 18616 will be Exhibit P580.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, P580 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter 10019. While we're waiting for that to come up, Your Honours, I would indicate that Ms. Stewart has assisted me in terms of the date in which the missing page was disclosed. It was disclosed on the 30th of November in batch 49, along with a note advising the Defence that this replaced the previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a time quite different from what you indicated earlier, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Not with respect to the B/C/S version of the statement, Your Honour, which, as I'd indicated, has always had that missing page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You have before you, sir, -- it we could concentrate on the top right-hand corner in English. A handwritten note on this document which reads, "Colonel Tadija gave partial reply." And the document is also written or dated the 26th of April, 1995. This purports to be a document written by commander Ratko Mladic to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. And again I'll read you portions and then I'll have some questions for you: "We are in possession of information that you are planning to use two air bombs against enemy targets and settlements in the area of Sarajevo in the evening or during the night of 26 April 1995. "You are to inform me whether the above-mentioned information is correct, who ordered and why, the planned use of heavy weapons and beginning of operations in the area of Sarajevo, if it is a question of retaliation and for what reason, or exploitation of operative effects. "If the Supreme Command has issued an order to begin the combat operations and use heavy weapons in the area of Sarajevo, it is your duty to inform me. "Before you begin with combat operations in the area Sarajevo, you are to provide me with a detailed report on planning, measures and goals in order to take a decision at the level of the Army of the Republika Srpska Main Staff." How does this document appear to compare with the exhibit we just introduced?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The two seem to be linked, and this document appears to reinforce the command of General Mladic on what activities happen in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In document -- sorry, from the previous document we learned that the decision to use weapons and to launch an attack on the tunnel had been made during the morning of the 26th of April, 1995, and we have a response from General Mladic that same day indicating that he's aware of this planned use. What does that tell you about the effectiveness or -- sorry, about his knowledge, General Mladic's knowledge, of what was occurring in his subordinate units in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object as it calls for speculation as to General Mladic's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What does that suggest to you about the information or communications system within the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From the two documents, it suggests to me that there is an information passage capability to General Mladic that is both timely and accurate, such that he is able to write this letter back down to the Romanija Corps before actions are supposed to happen. This all is happening in a day which suggests to me a very effective communication system of information passage and staffing and providing guidance to his subordinate corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Based on your interactions with the VRS, do you have any information as to how it would be possible if General Mladic wasn't copied on the previous order that he would be aware that this was -- planned operation was going to make place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: From my experience during this time, there were two chains of command. There was the operational chain of command, General Mladic to his corps commander. But there was also the extensive use of liaison officers embedded in those formations, i.e., the corps or the brigade, that reported directly back to General Mladic, for example, Major -- Colonel Indic was the liaison officer at the Romanija Corps whose -- his rank did not really indicate his influence, because he did not report to the corps commander. He responded to the direction from the army headquarters out of Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I'm looking at the clock. The Chamber intends to take a break now a bit more longer than usual so we have time for lunch. We would come back at 2.30 and that we would then have an extended session of 75 minutes being the last session for today. We resume at 2.30. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Ms. Bolton, you have got 42 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Fraser. Ms. Bolton will now continue her examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just before the break, General, we were discussing how there were in essence two chains of command and the role that liaison officers played and you said there was the operational chain of command, General Mladic to his corps commanders. In terms of the ability to, for example, control shelling or sniping or offensive military operations, is that something that lay with Colonel Indic or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That would be the responsibility of Generals Milosevic or Galic -- Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So when you're talking about operational command, it encompasses what?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It encompasses all the movement of troops or the action of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And based on your observations, General Indic was the source of information about what was happening in what, the corps, the brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Indic provided us information about what was the intentions of -- the headquarters out of Pale were. If we wanted to get a message out to General Mladic we could also tell Indic and he would relay that information up there, and he was essentially the eyes and ears of the army headquarters down in -- at the Romanija Corps. He was a -- for the most part a participant of all the meetings I attended with my commander with the Serbian corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I move for admission of the document we were discussing before the break which was 65 ter 10019.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 10019 will be Exhibit P581.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: While you were in Sarajevo, did the UNPROFOR or sector command have dealings with the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: My commander dealt with the UNMOs. They were not part of his chain of command. They reported directly up to Zagreb, but we would have regular correspondence and dialogue with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And would you share information in the terms of -- of their reports, for example?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We shared reports, so any of their investigations we would have received copies of them and vice versa. They were working out of the PTT building where my sector headquarters was located. And as I say, we didn't work for each other, but we would collaborate with information.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. May I have 65 ter 11192, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And while that's being brought up, General, I'm going to remind you of a portion of your statement at paragraph 130, and I'll read this for the Court so you don't need to look at -- display the statement. There you state: "During my testimony in Prosecutor versus Karadzic, I was shown document bearing ERN ET0528-8044-0528-8046, a regular combat report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The document was addressed to the Main Staff of the Army of the Republika Srpska and was signed by General Dragomir Milosevic. The document indicates that the Ilidza Brigade of the SRK launched a 250-kilogramme modified air bomb at the centre of Hrasnica on 7th April 1995. Hrasnica was essentially a civilian area (Muslim) at the foot of Mount Igman." Could I ask you now to look at the document on the screen before you, and could you tell me if you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who or what organisation authored this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This is a report from one of the UNMO teams.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the subject line says "Large EXP in Hrasnica on 7th April 95." What is EXP short for?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that we turn to page 2 in the English version of the document and also in the B/C/S version of the document. At -- sorry, if we could scroll up to the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's an indication there: "From BiH sources after the weapon was fired, the time of flight was approximately 20 seconds. The weapon left a trail of black smoke and was slow in flight." Could you tell me how that description compares with the description you received about the flight of modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have the right page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That would be consistent with the reports that we received of aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could I go back to page 1 in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's an indication at paragraph 2 that: "The weapon used is believed to be a homemade device consisting of an aircraft bomb and four 120-millimetre MBRL rockets." And then at paragraph 3 to the team retrieving several large pieces from the weapon including three 128-millimetre rocket bodies, the parts of a possible aircraft bomb fuse and three large steel plates. How do those components compare with descriptions of other modified air bombs you'd heard about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They are consistent with what the reports we were -- we were receiving of these air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I ask that this document be tendered as the next exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection from the Defence, Your Honours. This document was disclosed to us for the first time less than 24 hours ago. Seven days ago we received 28 new documents that had been previously undisclosed for this witness, many of whom were presented in proofing with this witness. This document was not on at that list, so we presume unless the witness brought this document with him it was unduly withheld by the Prosecution and [indiscernible] notice of it, and it's in violation of your guidance from previously as to documents for witnesses and when they should be disclosed to Defence. So I think on principle I have to stand on this document and object, given the nature of all the surprises we've had with this witness thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This document was referred to in the final paragraph of the e-mail that was sent on the 2nd of December, 2012. This was a document that I wasn't sure the witness was going to be able to speak to until it was shown to him, and so I wrote at that time and said for the benefit of the Defence and Trial Chamber, I'm also writing to advise that I anticipate discussing 65 ter 11192 with the witness during proofing. Depending on the witness's comments, this document may be included on the Prosecution's final list of exhibits which I anticipate producing as soon as proofing is complete. So there was notice as of Sunday that this was a potential exhibit for the witness, and I'm just going to wait for my -- Ms. Stewart to assist me in terms of the date of disclosure of this document to the Defence if I may have a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, is it on the 65 -- you mean the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit list. That is intended to be used as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, it's always had 11192. Is that what you're -- yes. Yes, Your Honour, I understand your question. And sorry, Your Honour, it was disclosed as part of batch 4 as part of a larger range, which would be -- and, sorry, I'm just going to get you the date it was uploaded into e-court. You will recall batch 4 was part of, I believe, the materials that were disclosed in the spring. Yes. And it's been available on e-court since the 25th of April, 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, it sounds as if you do not understand at all how when something was already -- was already given notice of the 2nd of December, which was Sunday, how Mr. Ivetic could even think about complaining. That's how it sounds, and that sounds similar to somewhere after the 2nd of October when you referred to, I think, the 30th of November. Of course, it's right, that is after the 2nd of October, but Mr. Ivetic referred to timely giving notice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, he referred to seeing it for the first time, I believe, yesterday, Your Honour, which is incorrect. It has been disclosed for months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In this context -- I think in this context that's how I understood his words. And he referred to the guidance of the Chamber. Have you any comments on that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. As I understand the guidance, we provide a list of documents seven days in advance that we are reasonably sure we're going to be introducing. Your guidance, though, has always indicated that there is some flexibility, because, of course, things come up during proofing which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but isn't it true that you presented this document to the witness during proofing so that you have prepared for proofing so that you would know what you'd put to the witness during proofing. And then to say that -- I mean, the witness didn't bring the document, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sure I'm not following Your Honour. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I didn't have any idea whether this could be introduced through this witness until it was shown to him during proofing Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you had selected it for proofing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On Sunday I selected this document for proofing and I immediately sent an e-mail to the Defence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it true that you gave notice already before the proofing that you intended to use this document during proofing?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. As soon as I located --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why had you not done that a couple of days before?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Because when I did my initial searches, Your Honour, the document didn't show up as being associated to this witness, and so once I found it by going through online our 65 ter list to see if we had documents relating to this incident, I located it and I notified the Defence as soon as it was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be marked for identification. Ms. Bolton, one of the problems with your explanation is that if that would happen with more documents that the element of surprise would take dimensions which are to be avoided. Please proceed. And the number, of course, should be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be P582 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General, can I move to the topic of shelling generally, not modified air bombs at this point. You indicate at paragraph 102 of your statement that after the February 1994 cease-fire agreement was signed, there was a decrease in the shelling in the city of Sarajevo. Could you tell us did there come a time when shelling began to increase again?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It did over time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time period it was that it started to pick up again?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It started to pick up again in the spring.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 120 and 121 of your statement, you describe the shelling of the Lukavica Barracks by the ABiH, and you describe that attack -- or, sorry, the BSA response to that attack as being indiscriminate and disproportionate. And you state that the barracks was a legitimate military target and there was no indication from "our troops that the ABiH shells were falling outside the barracks into civilian areas." When you refer to "our troops," who were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We had UN troops at the Lukavica Barracks complex, and initially when we received reports from them that the Serbian corps headquarters was being shelled we do admit we were surprised because this was the first time this had happened. We called back to the Bosnian corps headquarters and advised them to stop in the sense of because we knew what was going to happen, which did happen later that day, which Sarajevo received countless numbers of artillery rounds coming into the city not directed at -- at the Muslim Corps headquarters but they seemed to be random throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you indicate, sorry, that you had troops at the headquarters on that occasion, do you have any recollection as to approximately when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do not recall the actual date. I just recall the incident and the details of the incident because it was, as I say, the first time we had ever witnessed one side firing at a corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We can move on to the topic of sniping, sir. Paragraph 65 of your statement you refer to the fact that if someone picks up a weapon, then they become a military target, and if they use that weapon in an offensive manner towards the other side. An armed soldier is a legitimate military target. What about an unarmed soldier, somebody who is off duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: If somebody is wearing the uniform and can be identified as a soldier of the opposite side, they would be legitimate targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if they're not in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They would be for the -- I would constitute them as noncombatants and not a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 10 -- 10821, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: While that's being brought up, General, at paragraphs 90 to 94 of your statement, you've discussed the anti-sniping agreement that was entered into in August of 1994. Do you recall that agreement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On the screen before you, you should see a letter, and it's addressed to a Colonel Lugonja, security officer in the Romanija Corps. It's dated the 17th of August, 1994. And if we could scroll down to the bottom of the document, please, it's signed by Colonel Gausseres. Did you know Colonel Gausseres?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I knew Colonel Gausseres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And Colonel Lugonja?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I knew him, yeah. I knew him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this document refers at paragraph 2, second sentence indication that on your request: "There will be no anti-sniping team on your side, but you are expected not to retaliate if you don't want to worsen an already tense situation with as probable result a break of the deal agreed." Could you tell us what they're talking about when they're talking about putting an anti-sniping team on your side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The UN was responsible for protecting civilians on both sides of the confrontation line. Any actions between the two war factions was something the UN would not engage in directly, but when it came to civilians we would. As part of the anti-sniping agreement, we put into place an anti-sniping task force where we put UN troops on the Bosnian side, and we asked to put troops on the Serbian side. They refused, and this refers to their decision not to accept our anti-sniping task force on their side of the line.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did the duties of the anti-sniping task force include investigating alleged incidents of sniping against civilians?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was -- and determining the origin or probable origin of the shot or the fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It included determining where the point of shot came from, what was the result of that shot up to and including protesting to the applicable side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware, did the Bosnian Serbs ever explain why they wouldn't allow an anti-sniping team on their side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They never explained it to us, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is also a reference in paragraph 4, it states: "We will comply to your wish not [sic] to protect your trolley bus line ..." Was there any explanation -- sorry, when we talked about protecting a trolley bus line, what do you understand the UN was offering to do?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We were offering to put up protective barriers or putting anti-sniping forces there to prevent somebody from shooting at the trolley buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was any explanation offered as to why the Bosnian Serbs would refuse that offer?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: None was given to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether the sniping of civilians in BSA-held areas of Sarajevo was discussed in the Serbian or Bosnian Serbian media?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do recall at times when Serbian civilians were injured or killed we would read about it in the media and at times the Serbs would protest against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could this document be marked as the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P583.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have, please, 65 ter 10994. There are -- for the assistance of the Court the original here is in French and if we could have page 3 of the original document first. If we could scroll up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This document, sir, is from 4.0 Secteur de-Sarajevo [French spoken] do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is [French spoken]?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Infantry Battalion number 2 also referred to as FreBat 2 was one of the three French battalions. This one was at -- located at the airport and also assigned to provide the bulk of the anti-sniping task force.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we bring up the -- we have the English translation of this document on the screen. Could we bring up the B/C/S translation of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have two English versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, can counsel clarify which page in e-court. There is 11 pages total in the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's the -- I believe, the document you have on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar is asking for the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. No. I think she has the correct page displayed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, looking at the English translation of the FreBat report from the 14th of September, 1994, where there's an indication if we could scroll down, please, in both versions, of an investigation by the anti-sniping team into firing on the 6th September from a cannon coming from the Ilidza Terme Hotel at civilians crossing the bridge, and then again on the 2nd of September, 1994, again 20-millimetre cannon fired by the Serbs both at the population and two UNPROFOR vehicles. The weapon involved in this instant case is described as a 20-millimetre cannon. Could you tell us is that a specialised piece of sniping equipment?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if I could just tender this document then, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 0 -- 10994 will be Exhibit P584.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask for a video-clip bearing 65 ter 22329 to be played. I will indicate, Your Honour, that the Prosecution is not relying on the audio for this clip, just the visual, and it's only about 11 seconds in duration.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: "This was the moment. A second French peacekeeper is killed by a sniper while trying to erect protective barricades in Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said no audio. We only have audio but no video.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We're experiencing technical difficulties. I'll just give Ms. Stewart a moment to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it you do not want to rely on the spoken text?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't wish to rely on the text, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, sir, while we're waiting for that to be brought up, you describe at paragraph 88 of your statement an incident involving the death of an UNPROFOR soldier performing anti-sniping duties.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I recall it very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could watch, I think we're going to have the clip available in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We saw a very short clip there of sniper fire at a UN vehicle. Is this the incident you were describing in your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that incident took place?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I believe it was in April of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the video played and marked with 65 ter 22329 will be Exhibit P585.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P585 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The last subject area I want to discuss with you, General, is the situation in April 1994 when you first assumed your duties as a military assistant to the Sector Sarajevo commander. According to your statement, you arrived in Sarajevo on the 17th of April, 1994. And could you tell us if at the time of your arrival you were given any kind of briefing as to what had been going on?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I received a general briefing up in Zagreb from the Canadian headquarters and then moved down into Sarajevo and received a detailed briefing from the outgoing military assistant Christian de Bergeron.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was Mr. de Bergeron somebody who was known to you previously or did you just meet him in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I met him in Sarajevo but he was from the Canadian army and from the Van Doos regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recall what you were told and what the situation was on the ground when you arrived in Sarajevo with respect to freedom of movement for UNMOs, UNPROFOR, and humanitarian aid convoys?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I was informed that freedom of movement was limited and restricted and controlled by the warring factions, principally the Serbs. The situation in Sarajevo was dire given the siege that was going on, the shelling and sniping. And also at that time the enclaves were under significant pressure, and when I arrived principally it was -- the main effort was in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I please have 65 ter 10018.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at the English version of this document, sir, it's a document drafted it would appear by David Harland. Do you know Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is a number -- or are a number of acronyms used in the distribution list. Could you tell us whether this is a document that you and General Soubirou would have been privy to during your time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This is something he would have read.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I go to page 2, please, in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Starting at the top of the page under the heading "Gorazde crisis," it reads: "At about 1500 yesterday (16494) Bosnian lines to the north of Gorazde suddenly collapsed shortly after lines to the south-east of the town were also ruptured. "Advancing Serb forces overran an UNPROFOR observes post, injuring two UN observers, one of them critically." Skipping the next paragraph, it continues: "Shortly after 1800 a local cease-fire was arranged to allow for a helicopter evacuation of the wounded UN personnel. This was done but the soldier died shortly after arriving in Sarajevo." There's then a description at the bottom of the page about: "Gorazde has been reasonably quiet for several days following a second use of NATO airpower on Monday (11.4.94)." Could you tell us what prompted the use of NATO airpower in April of 1994 to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: With the collapse of the Gorazde pocket the concern was for the civilians inside of Gorazde and prompted the UN to ask for NATO strikes to keep -- to protect the civilians from what was coming in at them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And do you recall whether Gorazde had been declared a UN safe area at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's an indication on this page that General Mladic was verbally warned that airpower would be used if the shelling did not stop immediately. Later in the paragraph he says at 14.33 General Mladic was warned again, at 15.08 tank opened fire again in Gorazde, and then finally a fax is received from General Mladic assuring UNPROFOR that an order had been passed to cease-fire and the fire later subsided and no further action was taken. How does that information compare with the information you received when you were briefed on the situation?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It would be consistent with what de Bergeron and the French staff were giving me when I got there on the ground and listening to the updates received by General Soubirou but -- from his staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have page 3, please, in English and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: An indication on page 3 in English the third bullet point indicates UN UNPROFOR personnel have been seized throughout Serb-controlled territory. More than 150 UN personnel are in some way restricted in their movements on Serb territory. And then at six bullet point an indication that UNPROFOR has been blockaded in Sarajevo. Again, how does that compare with the situation you encountered when you arrived on the 17th of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is consistent. When I arrived, the situation was particularly grave with the actions inside of Gorazde focusing everyone's attention. And commensurate with that is just the freezing of the situation elsewhere. Particularly where I was in Sarajevo our freedom of movement was severely restricted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the fact that this was happening throughout Serb-controlled territory, what did that suggest to you in terms of the level of command that may have issued the instructions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Because of the geographical dispersion and the similarities of the activities throughout those areas, the Romanija Corps didn't control all this area. It would -- it did indicate to us that General Mladic's headquarters was controlling the operations and the control of movement of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have this document marked as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 10018 will be Exhibit P586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have one final document, sir, which is 65 ter 00113.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version just be shown -- moved over a little bit so we can see the left side of the page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just looking at the B/C/S version on the left side of the page you'll see that this appears to be marked as a telegram. Looking at the English version, it's document dated the 10th of April, 1994, issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, very urgent. It's addressed to the commands of a number of corps including the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could scroll down in the English version, please, it reads: "Based on the decision of the president of the Republika Srpska and the commander of the GS VRS and in order to make measures for the defence of Republika Srpska from the attacks of the NATO Air Force ..." If we could move to page 2 in English only, please: "I hereby order:" Paragraph 2 -- sorry, paragraph 4: "Immediately block all UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisation's convoys and their teams which happen to be in the Republika Srpska territory. Remove and secure the convoys and bring in the personnel and secure them at a safe place. Do not treat them roughly in the process." And could we turn to page 3 in English, please and to the last page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you'll notice that it is purported to be a document issued by a commander Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic. Is the treatment accorded humanitarian convoys and UN personnel that you were made aware of in April of 1994 consistent with what was ordered in this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: This document would verify, confirm the experience that we were having on the ground and also indicate that the restriction of movement by the UN and humanitarian aid was in violation of the terms why we were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be tendered as the next document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 00113 will be Exhibit P587.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P587 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That would conclude the Prosecution's time with the witness, Your Honour. I had indicated that there are three exhibits to be discussed, but I am content we do that after the witness has finished testifying, if that's agreeable to the Court. These are the three associated exhibits objected to by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not entirely clear what you mean by do that after the witness is testifying. Do you want to tender them from the bar table or --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. We would discuss it after he has been cross-examined and re-examined so he doesn't sit here while we make submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. I didn't follow the numbers, which are on the record. Mr. Ivetic, are you ready to start the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fraser, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Mladic Defence team. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir, before I begin with my questions I'd like to remind you that since we both speak English we need to work really hard to have a pause between question and answer to permit the court reporter and the translators to do their job. Is that understood, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that case I'd like to begin. The first area that I'd like to address is your consolidated statement which has been admitted as P576 and which I believe you still have a copy of in front of you. First of all, sir, could you tell me: Did you draft this statement or was it drafted for you by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It came from my previous statements. I reviewed it many times and made corrections before I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fraser, that's not exactly an answer to the question. The question was who drafted it and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- prepared it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prepared it. They gave the draft to me which I reviewed, amended, gave it back to them. They gave me back a revised draft, and at the end I signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The consolidated statement at pages 2 and 3 in the English, and I believe also the B/C/S, has an index. Were these topics or groupings generated by yourself or by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: In this draft it was generated by the Prosecutor based on my very first statement that I gave many years ago which I myself wrote out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say the statement -- the first statement that you gave many years ago that you wrote out, would that be the statement in 1997, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I note from the cover page of the consolidated statement that an individual by the name of Marija Dow from the CAF was present. Am I correct that this is a reference to the legal counsel for the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That person is Marla Dow, and she was a legal officer who was just there to observe the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I apologise. Was she there on behalf of the Canadian Armed Forces; that is to say, is CAF an acronym for the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did Ms. Dow, the legal counsel from the Canadian Armed Forces, intervene to direct any questions or direct any answers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No, she did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did legal counsel from the Canadian Armed Forces intervene to object to any question or answer which you provided to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No, she did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You indicated that the document was sent back with revisions and that the OTP sent a new version back to you and I note that the statement itself, the conversations took place in July, although the original copy was signed in October. Was the legal counsel from the Canadian Armed Forces involved in this revision process; that is to say, did it have to be vetted through them?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: She was part of the e-mail exchange, but she did not vet the document. She did not approve the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to now move to the time period before you were deployed to the former Yugoslavia. First of all, in your years of training and education to become a member of the Canadian Armed Forces, did you ever have a course of study with a focus on the structure or doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army or the Yugoslav All People's Defence system?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask one clarification on the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- few answers. You said, Mr. Fraser, that Ms. Dow was part of the e-mail exchange. That is not entirely clear to me. Was it that she was copied on the e-mails sent or did she actively participate in that e-mail exchange so as to suggest changes or whatever? Did she play an active role or was she just copied on everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was -- she was my conduit to the Prosecution. She played no role in modifying or advising me on the document. She was strictly as an observer to report what happened to the Canadian Forces, but she had no role in anything that I've written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. And she did not in any way suggest anything. She was just copied on it and would have done with it but not sent an e-mail, Have you not overlooked this, or, Isn't it true that Mr. Fraser also said, or nothing of the kind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She gave no counsel, no commentary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, the question I had asked was I'd like to move to the time period before you were deployed to the former Yugoslavia. In your years of training and education to become a member of the Canadian Armed Forces, did you ever have a course instructing or focusing on the structure and/or doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army or the Yugoslav All People's Defence system?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could focus now on the time period just before your deployment to Yugoslavia. Did you have any courses or instruction at that time relative to the structure or doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Army of Republika Srpska, or the Armija BiH, or the Croat Defence Union, the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I received no instruction other than the briefings I received when I arrived in theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's deal first with the briefings that you indicated -- you took part in in Zagreb. How long did those briefings last?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I recall probably two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what topics were covered in those briefings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
