utterances.text: The Canadian headquarters gave me general briefings on the country, the state of situation on the ground, and general information on the warring factions, plus what rules and regulations that I had to abide by, both as a Canadian and as a member of the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time of your first deployment to the former Yugoslavia, were you able to speak or understand any of the local languages of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Nothing other than the pleasant formalities of hello and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With -- with respect to the briefing now that you had with Mr. de Bergeron when you arrived in Sarajevo, first of all, am I correct that it was two days worth of briefings with Mr. de Bergeron as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I think we had probably about three or four days of briefings there and then that was direct one-on-one. In addition, I was briefed up by the UN staff, so each of the directors would sit down with the operations staff, the information staff, and the other branches to get up to speed on what was going on. Plus there was a French aide-de-camp, a Captain Deduc [phoen], who was also there and remained as the continuity who also give me briefings on what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to 65 ter 1D457 briefly. And while we wait for that, sir, I believe this would be the 1997 statement that both you and I had discussed earlier. I see that the English is already up on the screen. Does this cover sheet or cover page refresh your recollection or can you clarify that this is the statement that you discussed earlier that you wrote in 1997?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is that your signature at the bottom of the English original?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn page 2 in both languages and I'd like to focus on the second-to-last paragraph. And do you see there, sir, it says: "I did not receive any briefings about my new posting in Bosnia until after I got there. I had two days with Christian de Bergeron and then he was gone." Could you explain for me which version is true? You've mentioned briefings before arriving to Bosnia --

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No. What I said was when I got --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly reminded to observe the pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived in Zagreb, that's when I got the briefings from the Canadian headquarters. So that's when I received the briefings, when I got to Bosnia, not when I was in Canada. And then when I got down into Sarajevo, that's when Bergeron -- you know, he and I talked for those couple days, and I talked to the headquarters. That's when I received the briefings. So I am consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I misunderstood your reference to the Canadian headquarters. I'd like to ask you with respect to the briefings that you had with Mr. de Bergeron, did any of those briefings detail the normative structures or doctrine of the JNA, the VRS, or the Armija BiH?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: They did talk about the fact that I would be dealing with a corps headquarters. There were brigades in around Sarajevo. They talked about the Muslim Corps structure and the army structures in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long had your predecessor Mr. de Bergeron been in Sarajevo by that point, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I believe he was there about a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say that you discussed army structures in "general terms." Did any of the briefings entail a discussion or identification of the specific locations within the city of Sarajevo where the Armija BiH had troops situated?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That information existed in the headquarters. My focus was on the headquarters of the two warring factions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any of your briefings with Mr. de Bergeron entail a discussion or identification of military depots or storage facilities that were located within the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We talked about the weapon collecting points.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about weapons -- munitions depots or storage facilities apart from the weapons collection points?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: That I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that any such military depots or supply storage facilities, apart from the weapons collection points, would constitute legitimate military targets even if located in the depth of territory behind the front lines in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: As a hypothetical question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if your briefings with Mr. de Bergeron included discussions about the location of any military production factories in or near the city limits of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I -- I don't recall those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, would you agree that any such production facilities or factories would likewise constitute legitimate targets even if behind the front lines in the depth of territory in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Hypothetically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you feel that -- that at the end of your briefing with Mr. de Bergeron you had sufficient information to fully perform all of the duties required of you as MA for the sector commander?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would now like to take some time to address portions of your consolidated statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So I would ask for P576 to be called up in e-court, and if we can look at paragraph 32 of the same, which is page 11 in the English and page 12 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you identify a Major Milenko Indjic as being the conduit between Generals Mladic and Tolimir and the corps commander and that: "His job is to ensure that the corps commander were acting in accordance with orders issued by the Main Staff." First of all, did you at any time ever speak with General Mladic or General Tolimir and have them explicitly tell you that Major Indjic served such a function or role as you have described here?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I never had a conversation with Generals Tolimir or Mladic about that. It was our observation based on what we experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did either Generals Galic or Milosevic ever confirm for you the role of Major Indjic to be as you have indicated in this paragraph of your statement, paragraph 32?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I do recall that he was referred to as the LO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thank you for that answer. Now could you answer my question. Did either Generals Galic or Milosevic ever confirm for you the role of Major Indjic to be as you have indicated in paragraph 32 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: We never had that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any officer of the VRS ever confirm for you the role of Major Indjic to be what you have listed in paragraph 32?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the one difference between Major Indjic and the other officers in the room was that he was fluent in English?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: He -- yes, from -- from my memory, he was the only one who could speak English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you permit the possibility that he was there precisely for his knowledge of the English language, to act as a means of being able to communicate more equally with the English-speaking international officers who would be present for meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: He was used for that, but his role was larger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many times were you present for meetings when Major Indjic and General Mladic were both present where Major Indjic appeared to be acting in the manner that you have described in paragraph 32?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: I don't recall specifically with that question, because I don't -- I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. If we can turn to paragraph 35 of your statement. This will be on page 12 of the English and page 13 of the Serbian. And here -- here you state that Milosevic was adhering to the orders issued by Mladic and that he understood that he served at the pleasure of General Mladic, and if he did not do as Mladic wanted, he would be replaced. Did you ever attend a meeting either in person or via telephone to hear General Mladic make such a statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: No. That was my inference based on meetings that I had attended with my sector commander and the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could clarify in your answer. You say "the general." Which general are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: General Milosevic and General Soubirou or Gobillard later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that General Milosevic never once made a statement to you indicating that he understood that he served at the pleasure of General Mladic, and if he did not do as General Mladic wanted he would be replaced as you have written in paragraph 35 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: He never said that. I inferred that from his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can look at paragraph 27 of this same consolidated statement. That would be at page 10 in the English and page 11 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you mention the airport tunnel and the Igman road. First of all, are you talking about both of these features when you indicate that it was used by both civilian and ABiH personnel and was subject to frequent shelling?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: It was used by both.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My question was which "it"? Are we talking about the Igman road or the airport tunnel or both?

utterances.speaker: DAVID FRASER
utterances.text: The Igman road and airport tunnel were used by both civilians and ABiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. We are supposed to finish at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honours. We can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Fraser, before we take a break, I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already today or that is testimony still to be given. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, are you on track at this moment as far as time is concerned? It's a bit early, but -- to ask, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thus far I'm on track for the time I had allotted for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And your estimate was that you needed four and a half hours, if I'm correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought it was four hours, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Four hours is what I was planning on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's how matters stand now. Then we -- which means that most likely we need the whole of tomorrow for this witness and then Friday we could continue with the witness next in line. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 6th of December, at 9.00 in the morning in this same Courtroom II.
